description: Sighting and photos (c) philhick.

MAINLAND QUOKKA
Many people know about the famous, small friendly herbivorous macropod from Rottnest Island, as you've no doubt seen from varying "Quokka selfies" taken there. There are quite a few on this island that unfortunately have become accustomed to humans so such a thing is possible than to walk up to a quokka a take a selfie with it. 
But did you know there are fragmented populations still on the mainland? And are struggling to survive. These mainland populations are spread out from bushland in the Perth Hills to outside Albany in the south. Currently listed as "Vulnerable" under IUCN 3.1 these species are being affected by predation from feral cats and foxes, habitat loss and changing fire patterns. 
And it's these fire pattern the people at DBCA (Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions) are currently monitoring in bushland outside Perth
Over the past few days I've been volunteering my time helping set traps, radio track current collared quokka, set up remote camera units while walking through some of our great forests outside Perth.. 
This was one male quokka of a hefty 5kg that we caught in a wildlife trap this morning. Weighed, tagged and collared to monitor movements through prescribed burning programs. Here Murdoch University PhD. candidate L. Povh is releasing said male who tore off into the bush as fast as his legs could carry him (which was pretty darn quick!). To reduce stress on the animal (which has never come into contact with humans before) all work was done inside this bag and it was released without much fuss (hence no quokka selfie ;) ).

I was walking east along the Wantirna South cycleway towards Knox City Shopping centre, and noticed a family was looking confused at a squirming shape, a bat, wrapped in white netting on a cherry tree. The net was illegal - white plastic, holes 2cm square (change this year to 5mm holes so birds and bats aren't snagged.....).
The bat was caught at the top-left, on the inside of a hole it seemed to have torn to get to the ripe cherries, struggling to free itself. The family had a short ladder, thick gardening gloves and a net on a pole however looked confused and uncertain. 

I offered my assistance, asking for a towel to wrap the bat and some scissors to cut the net - the father returning with a T-shirt and the scissors, and I climbed the ladder to see a Grey-headed Flying Fox struggling. As it noticed me it turned, looking me in the eyes and I noticed, with surprise, a plump, ripe, juicy cherry lodged firmly in its mouth, half out, and it munching away - although struggling in the netting, the flying fox was still eating cherries!

I folded the T-shirt in half length-ways and, reaching forward, wrapped it gently around the now vigorously struggling and shrieking flying fox, still munching on the cherry between shrieks. It calmed immediately with it's head covered - I bent the cherry tree limb towards me and to the father on the right, and he gently cut the net around the flying fox with scissors, keeping clear of the tangles around its legs.

I descended the ladder and carried the calm bundle close to the tall Eucalypt trees to the south of the cycleway, lowering it onto the grass, and carefully cut the netting away - it took a few minutes, tangled tight in a few places around the flying foxes legs. I checked the flying fox wasn't injured, gently moving the legs aside, then the arms and wings, relieved to see its arms and legs OK, no cuts in the wing membrane (the head still covered and flying fox calm and still) then took the shirt away with the flying fox in the grass. I immediately realised my mistake as it clumsily crawled over the grass towards a tree - they can't walk! I put the T-shirt over it again, picked it up and put it on a tree trunk, holding it until it got a firm hold with its claws, the T-shirt slipping free from its head. It climbed up steadily, clearly no injuries, webbing on its wings OK. I didn't take any photos at the time, the family took some and videos on their mobiles as I worked - their kids were happy it was free.

I came back later with a camera to take these photos of it comfortably at the top of the tree, moving into a roosting position. The last shot shows finally, its adventures complete, having found a comfortable position, and full of tasty cherries, it's nap time for the tired Grey-headed Flying Fox.

I stopped by next morning before dawn - it was gone, so hopefully OK and back with its family.

You can see why they called it a Flying Fox - it looks like a fox with wings.

description: (From Notes Taken At The Time): "Well, the very first Mammal I saw after nightfall was the one rumoured to be here that I’d spent the entire lead up of the trip telling myself I’d have no chance of seeing. I was just reaching the main stand of forest, quite literally only two trees in, when I just happened to do a sweep with the headlamp… wait!! Wait!!! There, crouched on one of the sturdy boughs exactly like a Squirrel, its fur glowing the most astounding shade of purply-bluish pearl, was a creature that struck me vividly in the moment as being like an exact cross between a Squirrel and a Bilby, with big, slightly pointy Bat-ears, a very pointed snout and… and… I actually cursed in shock and absolute disbelief when I saw the gigantic, impossibly fuzzy black brush of a tail trailing proudly out behind it!! There, peering down at me without an ounce of fear by a great deal of curiosity, was none other than a PHASCOGALE!!!! The next ten minutes were the best I’ve ever spent with a Mammal on land, hands down; it was like the Phascogale was very poorly playing peek-a-boo, its unquenchable curiosity making it unable to resist scuttling closer and peering out at me with those almost purplish-shining eyes, no matter how much my movements initially startled it… it moved, once again, astonishingly similarly to a Squirrel, racing with quicksilver litheness around the trunks and branches of the trees, totally happy to cling on upside down if it had to!!! It also occasionally looked for food in a most novel way; it sit in its Squirrel-pose, then frantically paw at the bark with its front feet, digging out any bugs that might be hiding!!! I ended up leaving it be long before it lost interest in me… and so the Phascogale passed into the pages of absolute history and truly joyful memories!!!"

description:
⭐
My girlfriend had an egg (or so she said, I never saw such egg).

We don't know what to do with an egg, so I thought about asking for help to the birds and the reptiles, but the language barrier between us was too big, they did not speak mammal. 

"Only if there was a mammal who lay eggs that we could talk to", I cried! And just a second after, I heared a familiar voice saying: -"They are the only mammals that lay eggs". I turn around and I saw that Ferb was talking from the inside of a TV, as he looked at Perry the Platypus. 
I inmediatly put on my boots and grabbed my girlfriend's hand, and we started running towards the river, to meet the mammal Ferb talked about.

We arrived around 7 in the morning and shortly after the platypus appeared, peeping out from the brown water. I screamed at him from the bridge, I cried that I needed advice about what to do with my girlfriend's egg. 
As I yelled I could see on his tiny mammal eyes that he could understand me, yet he said nothing. 

I kept crying for advice, and he just floated as liveless piece of wood, hoarding on all his egg related indigenous wisdom... infront of my despair.
 Bloody creature... Fucking selfish bloody creature. I curse you, Perry the Platypus!

Bandicoots never occupied a lot of space in my imagination. I knew they existed, I liked them, but I never dedicated daydreams and devotion to them.

Now I think often about bandicoots, now they live in my fantasies.

Usually this process happens on the opposite order: I obsess about an animal and I decide to go on a quest to find them until eventually they reveal themselves.
This time, an animal foreing to my fixations revealed himself and now is weighting heavy inside me, pooping in the folds of my brain and digging on my grey matter.

I highly recommed this experience.
